books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Ulysses S. Grant, Personal Memoirs, Chapter III, 1885

stimulus.source_note: Ulysses S. Grant, Personal Memoirs, Chapter III, published 1885. Public domain.
stimulus.text:
Generally, the officers of the army were indifferent whether the annexation was consummated or not; but not so all of them. For myself, I was bitterly opposed to the measure, and to this day regard the war, which resulted, as one of the most unjust ever waged by a stronger against a weaker nation. It was an instance of a republic following the bad example of European monarchies, in not considering justice in their desire to acquire additional territory.

The Southern rebellion was largely the outgrowth of the Mexican war. Nations, like individuals, are punished for their transgressions. We got our punishment in the most sanguinary and expensive war of modern times.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: A historian using Grant's memoirs as evidence about the Mexican War should keep in mind which of the following?

options.text: Grant wrote the memoirs during the war, so they record what soldiers thought at the time.
options.misconception: Grant wrote the memoirs in 1884-1885, nearly forty years after the war, as he was dying.

options.text: Grant never served in Mexico, so his account is based entirely on other men's stories.
options.misconception: Grant served as a young lieutenant in Mexico under Taylor and Scott.

options.text: Grant wrote decades later, looking back on the war through the Civil War and his presidency.
Grant's memoirs were written to defend Polk's decision to go to war.
options.misconception: Grant attacks Polk's war as unjust; the memoirs defend nothing about Polk's decision.

rationales.A: The memoirs were written in 1884-1885, forty years after the war, not during it.
rationales.B: Grant served in Mexico as a young officer; he was there himself.
rationales.C: Writing in 1885, after commanding the Union armies and serving two terms as president, Grant judged the Mexican War in light of the Civil War it helped bring on.
rationales.D: Grant calls the war unjust; his memoirs are a condemnation of Polk's war, not a defense of it.
rationales.general:
1. Check the date. The memoirs appeared in 1885, when Grant was dying, forty years after Mexico.
2. Ask what those forty years added. Grant had commanded the Union armies and served as president, and he saw the Civil War as the price of the Mexican War.
3. Use the memoir for what it is: a veteran's later judgment, powerful as reflection, not a diary of 1846.
Remember: a memoir's date is its lens — Grant writes about 1846 with the whole Civil War behind his eyes.
